questions.text: According to acoustic mass law, doubling the mass of a wall assembly increases sound transmission isolation by approximately ___ dB.

options.text: Cannot increase; doubling mass reduces frequency response

rationale.a: 3 dB is half the increase; incorrect.
rationale.c: 12 dB is double the increase; overstates relationship.
rationale.d: Mass increase always improves isolation; frequency response becomes less important at higher mass.
rationale.correct: Mass law: every doubling of mass increases sound isolation by approximately 6 dB. A 100 kg/m² wall at STC 40 becomes approximately STC 46 when mass is doubled to 200 kg/m².
rationale.takeaway: Mass law: +6 dB per doubling of mass. For high STC ratings (70+), mass alone is insufficient; damping (decoupling, absorptive fill) is required.

questions.text: STC (Sound Transmission Class) rating range is typically ___, with higher values indicating better sound isolation through walls.

options.text: 0-1.0 (0-100%), which is not applicable to STC ratings as they are not percentage-based
20-50 dB, which is a common range for residential and commercial buildings
NRC 0.3-0.9, which refers to sound absorption rather than transmission

rationale.a: 0-1.0 is NRC (sound absorption rating), not STC (isolation).
rationale.b: dB is a unit; STC is not expressed in dB directly (though it relates to sound reduction in dB).
rationale.correct: STC is a single-number rating 50-80 (higher = better isolation). A wall with STC 50 blocks average speech; STC 70 blocks loud music.
rationale.takeaway: STC = sound isolation (wall assembly property); NRC = sound absorption (interior finish property). STC 50-80; NRC 0-1.0.

questions.text: In tropical residential design, bulk fiberglass insulation is often supplemented or replaced with reflective barriers (aluminum foil or white coating) because ___.

options.text: Reflective barriers cost less than bulk insulation, which is not always the case depending on material quality.
Radiant heat is the dominant heat gain mechanism; reflectivity reduces absorbed solar radiation more effectively than k-value
Fiberglass is not fire-resistant in tropical climates, which is a misconception as it is generally fire-resistant.
Reflective barriers improve acoustic isolation, although their primary function is thermal management.

rationale.a: Cost comparison is secondary; performance is primary criterion.
rationale.d: Reflective barriers reflect light; acoustic performance is independent of reflectance.
rationale.correct: Tropical solar radiation creates radiant heat gain (70-80% of total heat load). Reflectivity (emissivity reduction) from white/aluminum surfaces is more effective than bulk insulation k-value reduction. High albedo (reflectance) of light-colored roofing reduces surface temperature from 65°C to 45°C, dramatically reducing convective heat transfer.
rationale.takeaway: Tropical climates: reflective surfaces > bulk insulation for cooling. Conversely, temperate cold climates prioritize bulk insulation (k-value) for heating resistance.

questions.code_citation: Tropical Building Science, ASHRAE Climate Design Guide

questions.text: Extruded polystyrene (XPS) foam has k = 0.025 W/(m·K). What is the R-value of a 75 mm thick XPS layer?

rationale.b: Calculation error or different thickness assumed.
rationale.d: 1.5 reflects half the correct value; division error.
rationale.correct: R = thickness / k = 0.075 m / 0.025 W/(m·K) = 3.0 m²·K/W (option b). 1.875 would be for 47 mm thickness (0.047/0.025=1.88).
rationale.takeaway: R = thickness (m) / k-value. XPS k ≈ 0.025 W/(m·K). Memorize: 25 mm XPS ≈ R-1, 50 mm ≈ R-2, 75 mm ≈ R-3, 100 mm ≈ R-4.

questions.code_citation: ASTM C518, XPS Foam Material Data

questions.text: The formula relating R-value to k-value and thickness is ___.

options.text: R = k / thickness, which is incorrect as it does not account for the inverse relationship between R-value and k-value
R = k × thickness, which would imply a direct proportionality that does not exist in thermal resistance calculations
R = 1 / k, which ignores the role of material thickness in determining thermal resistance

rationale.c: Multiplication does not account for heat flow physics.
rationale.d: Reciprocal of k alone ignores thickness dimension.
rationale.correct: R = thickness (m) / k-value (W/(m·K)); this yields R-value in m²·K/W. Higher k yields lower R; thicker material yields higher R.
rationale.takeaway: R = thickness / k. Remember: higher k (poorer insulator) → lower R. Thicker material → higher R.

questions.text: Calculate the overall U-value for a wall assembly: interior air film (R = 0.12 m²·K/W), gypsum board (R = 0.10), 100 mm XPS insulation (k = 0.025), masonry (R = 0.25), exterior air film (R = 0.03). Assume XPS R = 100 mm / 0.025 = 4.0 m²·K/W.

rationale.a: 0.500 reflects inverse calculation or omitted insulation R-value.
rationale.c: 0.050 is over-conservative and reflects 1/20 instead of 1/4.5.
rationale.d: 2.0 indicates poor insulation; error in assembly calculation.
rationale.correct: R_total = 0.12 + 0.10 + 4.0 + 0.25 + 0.03 = 4.5 m²·K/W. U = 1 / R_total = 1 / 4.5 = 0.222 W/(m²·K). This indicates moderate thermal resistance; a well-insulated wall in tropical climates (where heating is not required) would target U < 0.5.
rationale.takeaway: U = 1 / R_total. Calculate total R by summing all layers including air films. Lower U-value indicates better insulation.

questions.text: A coastal tropical office specifies fiberglass batts (k = 0.040 W/(m·K)) for exterior cavity insulation. After 2 years of salt-spray and high-humidity exposure (80% RH), moisture absorption causes hygroscopic degradation. If fiberglass R-value decreases by 25% due to moisture, what is the performance loss? (Assume 100 mm fiberglass R = 2.5 initially.)

options.text: R-value remains 2.5 (moisture does not affect thermal performance)
R-value decreases to 1.25 (50% loss; moisture increases k-value)

rationale.a: Moisture dramatically affects fiberglass performance; R-value always decreases in humid climates.
rationale.c: 50% loss overstates typical moisture effect (25-40% degradation is typical for coastal fiberglass over 2-5 years).
rationale.d: Water has high thermal conductivity; moisture reduces R-value, not increases it.
rationale.correct: Initial R = 100 mm / 0.040 = 2.5 m²·K/W. Hygroscopic moisture absorption increases effective k-value (water conducts heat at ~0.6 W/(m·K), much higher than air). 25% R-loss: new R = 2.5 × 0.75 = 1.875 m²·K/W. This represents 25% degradation in thermal resistance, reducing effective insulation value significantly over 2 years.
rationale.takeaway: Fiberglass is hygroscopic; avoid in humid/coastal tropical zones without vapor barriers. Closed-cell polyurethane foam (low permeability) is superior in tropical maritime environments.

questions.code_citation: Moisture Effects on Fiberglass Insulation, Coastal Building Science

questions.text: Polyisocyanurate foam (polyiso) has a lower k-value than XPS, providing approximately ___ R-value per inch thickness compared to XPS.

rationale.a: Inverse relationship; polyiso has lower k, therefore higher R.
rationale.c: Relationship cannot be determined from k-value alone (false premise).
rationale.d: k-value is material-independent of thickness; R depends on both.
rationale.correct: Polyiso k ≈ 0.020 W/(m·K) vs XPS k ≈ 0.025 W/(m·K). R per inch: XPS = 25.4 mm / 0.025 = 1.016 m²·K/W ≈ 5.8 per inch (imperial units), polyiso ≈ R-6.5 per inch (k imperial ≈ 0.14 Btu·in/(hr·ft²·°F)) vs XPS R-5.0 (k≈0.18). Polyiso provides higher R per thickness due to lower k-value.
rationale.takeaway: k-value hierarchy: polyiso (0.020) < XPS (0.025) < fiberglass (0.040). Lower k → higher R per inch. Polyiso is most efficient; highest cost.

questions.code_citation: ASTM C518, Foam Insulation Material Comparison

questions.text: NRC (Noise Reduction Coefficient) rating of 0.7 indicates that the material absorbs ___ percent of incident sound.

options.text: Cannot be determined from NRC alone

rationale.d: NRC directly indicates absorption percentage; can be determined.
rationale.correct: NRC 0.7 = 70% sound absorption. NRC 0 = 0% absorption (hard reflective surface); NRC 1.0 = 100% absorption (theoretical maximum).
rationale.takeaway: NRC 0-1.0 directly scales to absorption %: NRC 0.6 = 60%, NRC 0.8 = 80%, etc. NRC >0.7 required for effective noise control in open-plan offices.

questions.text: Thermal conductivity (k-value) is measured in ___ and is material-specific (independent of thickness).

rationale.b: m²·K/W is R-value (thermal resistance), which depends on thickness.
rationale.c: Btu·in/(hr·ft²·°F) is imperial k-value; correct units but less commonly used in metric regions.
rationale.d: Temperature gradient is not a unit of conductivity.
rationale.correct: k-value is thermal conductivity in W/(m·K) per ASTM C518; it describes material's ability to conduct heat, independent of thickness.
rationale.takeaway: k = thermal conductivity (material property, independent of thickness). R = thermal resistance (depends on thickness and k).
